analysis.one_liner: Ends major oil companies' tax breaks and offshore royalty relief, directing savings to deficit reduction.
analysis.headline: The Senate voted 52-48 to begin debate on the bill on May 17, 2011, short of the 60 votes needed, so it never came to a vote on its merits.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would take away five federal tax breaks from the largest oil companies — those with over $1 billion in annual revenue and at least 500,000 barrels of daily worldwide production — including a domestic manufacturing deduction, intangible drilling cost write-offs, and the percentage depletion allowance. It would also repeal a law letting the Interior Department suspend royalties on deep-water offshore oil and gas production. All savings would go to reducing the federal deficit or debt.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who would benefit from deficit reduction funded by removing tax breaks the bill's findings say gave oil companies more than $40 billion over the prior decade. The bill also states its purpose as responding to high gas prices, though the tax changes themselves would not directly lower pump prices.

how_it_helps.text: Denies five tax provisions to major integrated oil companies: the foreign tax credit for payments that are really royalties, the domestic production deduction for oil and gas income, the intangible drilling and development costs deduction, the percentage depletion allowance, and the tertiary injectants deduction.
Repeals Energy Policy Act sections 344 and 345, ending the Interior Secretary's authority to grant royalty relief for deep-water oil and gas and deep natural gas wells in the Outer Continental Shelf.
Dedicates all net savings to reducing the federal budget deficit or the public debt, and makes the bill comply with the Statutory Pay-As-You-Go Act.
The bill's findings state that major oil companies collected more than $40 billion in tax breaks over the prior ten years while amassing over $1 trillion in profits.

analysis.who_pays: The largest oil companies, which would pay higher federal taxes and, for new offshore leases, full royalties rather than reduced ones. Some of that cost could be passed through to consumers at the pump.

drawbacks.text: Raising the tax bill of the largest oil producers could raise costs that get passed to consumers in fuel prices, at least partially offsetting the deficit savings.

Some of the provisions are ordinary features of the tax code that apply beyond oil; removing them only for the biggest oil companies treats the same activity differently across industries, which supporters of the industry argue disadvantages U.S. companies against foreign state-owned rivals.

The bill would not directly lower gas prices; it responds to high prices largely by raising revenue and expressing a sense of the Senate, and its own findings project that expanded domestic drilling would cut gas prices by only about 3 cents per gallon by 2030.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill raises roughly $2 billion a year in revenue for deficit reduction at the cost of higher taxes on an industry that can absorb them — its own findings cite $40 billion in tax breaks over a decade against more than $1 trillion in profits. The main honest objection is pass-through to pump prices and the uneven treatment of the same tax provisions across industries, but the fiscal benefit to the public is real and the cost to consumers is likely modest.

outcome.mechanism: A vote to simply start debate on the bill needed 60 senators and got only 52, so the Senate never reached a vote on the bill itself.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 10, 2011 and placed on the Senate calendar the next day without any committee action.
On May 17, 2011, Majority Leader Reid made a motion to proceed to consideration of the bill — the step that opens debate on the floor.
The motion to proceed failed 52-48, short of the 60 votes required to end a filibuster of the motion, and the motion was withdrawn.
The vote split by party: 48 of 51 Democrats, 2 of 47 Republicans, and both independents present voted yes; 45 of 47 Republicans and 3 Democrats voted no.
Because the Senate never took up the bill, no vote on its merits ever occurred and it died at the end of the 112th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major oil companies kept the tax breaks and offshore royalty relief the bill would have removed, and the deficit got no offsetting revenue from them. Senators who opposed it avoided a recorded vote on the substance, since the bill never reached the floor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Major oil companies, which kept their tax breaks

sides.party_line_note: On the only vote taken, 48 of 51 Democrats voted to begin debate while 45 of 47 Republicans voted against it; two Republicans and all independents present crossed over, leaving the bill three votes short of the 60 needed.

industries.note: The bill would deny them five tax breaks, including the domestic production deduction and percentage depletion, and its findings say the industry collected over $40 billion in such breaks over ten years. The industry's gain in keeping them comes directly at the cost of federal revenue that would otherwise reduce the deficit.

industries.industry: Deep-water offshore oil and gas producers
industries.note: The bill repeals the Interior Secretary's authority to suspend royalties on deep-water and deep-gas Outer Continental Shelf production, so new leases would pay full royalties instead of discounted ones. Suspending royalties shifts public revenue to leaseholders.
